utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. As usual, I put the question to you: Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, may it please Your Honours, my name is Andrew Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my colleague Anna Richterova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman and I appear with my co-counsel Milka Maglov and Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. And for General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. I am Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and I'm assisted by Fabien Masson. I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. So are there any preliminaries that you would like to have discussed or debated before we call in the witness? Okay. So Madam Registrar, someone perhaps could bring the witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Medic. You will be handed once more the same piece of paper as yesterday in which there is the solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to make before you recommence giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down and good morning to you. This morning, you are going to be cross-examined first by the Defence counsel for General Momir Talic. Later on you may or may not be cross-examined by the other Defence team, that is for Radoslav Brdjanin. I can't tell you as from now what's going to happen. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before starting I would like to demand the Prosecutor to provide the witness with his statements, former statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could take the statements? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make sure that he has the right statements. Mr. Medic

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have three statements? One from January, 1996, one from August, 2001 and your written statement of February, 2000?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, you should have in front of you one statement which allegedly you made following the interviews on the 30th and 31st of January, 1996. Do you have that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have it in the -- your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you should have another statement which dates 24th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, do you have it in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is another statement made supposedly by you on the 22nd of February, 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have it in your own language, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then Madam Fauveau, I think on the basis of that you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, you had two interviews with the Prosecutor's Office, once in January, 1996 and the second time in August 2001. You also provided a written statement in February, 2000. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you provided this written statement, the one that you wrote in February, 2000, at the request of the Prosecutor or was it on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of August, 2001, on page 2, you said that you had an interview with the Prosecutor but that you hadn't made a signed, written statement or rather that you hadn't signed your statement. On page 2 of your statement that you gave in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the third paragraph. You said that you had previously been interviewed by the Prosecutor but that you didn't sign a statement. Mr. Medic, have you found this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the text. You have to tell me what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the statement of August, 2001, and in your language, it starts with, "MKSJ already interviewed me but I didn't give a signed statement."

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it now. I can see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at the written -- at the English version of your declaration of 1996, it has been signed Adil Medic. Mr. Medic, it's the text that is English. I think it is to your right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there was an exchange where I wrote that I had personally submitted a statement, but that doesn't change anything. It's true that in January, 1996, I gave a statement to the investigators. I gave a statement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you did sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also signed the statement that you wrote in February, 2000?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you wrote your statement in February, 2000, did you use certain documents to verify the names or the dates that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put certain elements into order in my head and on paper so perhaps certain dates had to be corrected, but they were small corrections. But nothing essential is changed by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the activities of Merhamet restarted in 1991, in December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that before December, 1991, the Merhamet organisation was not active in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, what happened in December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a participant in that event but I know that it took place since there was a war in Croatia, they probably -- people probably thought that problems might arise. That the population might have to move and that they would need to be helped. That's my -- that's what I'm convinced of but I wasn't a participant in that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that the Red Cross existed in Banja Luka but that in 1992, it didn't communicate with the Serbian and Muslim people. Were you talking about the local Red Cross or the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say in 1991. I said in 1992. And I'm referring to the local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the International Red Cross was present in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992, I think that it was in the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after July, 1992, the International Red Cross was in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: From July, 1992, did you have contact with the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, continually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Merhamet have contact with the SDA in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, but the contact was sporadic and it was without me because I didn't take part in these contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the relation was between Merhamet and the SDA in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't very courteous.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were sometimes personal issues which were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that Merhamet helped in general Bosniak people, but that on your list, there were also 4.500 people of non-Muslim nationality. Do you have this list?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But in Merhamet -- this list existed in Merhamet, and they regularly received help at the -- at certain points, or as we call them Djemac [phoen], which is where they lived. Everyone lived together regardless of their nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this list still exists in Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it does. If it hasn't been taken away by -- in some sort of search.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of February, 2000, could you have a look at page 1? Your written statement, the one that you provided to the Prosecutor in written form.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, the very first paragraph, you said that General Talic phoned the mufti Halilovic to prepare a delegation in order to help the detainees in Manjaca because they did not have enough food.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or someone else from Merhamet contact General Talic before the telephone conversation with the mufti on the 16th of June?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that Mr. Alija Efendi Hadzihalilovic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in June, 1992, Banja Luka was not sufficiently provided with food and with medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, at the beginning, there was food, but there wasn't enough medicine, but as time passed, this lack increased. There was no alcohol at all, for example, and in medicine, that is essential.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 18th of June, 1992, the delegation of which you were a part visited the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Dr. Smajic should have been in this delegation but that he was prevented from doing so because he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the executive committee or board at the level of Yugoslavia and on the 17th, we had a meeting, a joint meeting, the entire team, and he gave us some very important instructions for our talks in Manjaca but unfortunately he wasn't able to go because he was prevented by being on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you can confirm that Dr. Smajic was prevented from visiting Manjaca camp and was prevented from doing this because of his work?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say where Dr. Smajic worked?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the psychiatric clinic. He's a neuropsychiatrist, I think. That's his profession, his specialty.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Dr. Smajic is a Muslim or a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The correction was good. I object to the term a Muslim, even in these documents, but, yes, he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During this first visit at the Manjaca camp, did you see the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to speak to them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions. Once while visiting the camp and the second time after a group had been taken out, a group of prisoners had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been taken out, seven from each stable.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during this visit, you spoke to Muhamed Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was immobile. He was the only one lying down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Muhamed Filipovic told you that he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say when he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't such opportunity for conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were the guards present while were you speaking to Muhamed Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers were nearby. The officers who were at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they able to hear your conversation with Muhamed Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So, in fact, you had the opportunity to speak to him in private, to the prisoners in private?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the people in the camp were dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You recognised certain people from the Kljuc area, in particular from Sanica?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see these people for the last time, before -- before you saw them in the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Banja Luka but at least once or twice I would spend my weekends in Sanica, at least once or twice a month. And I would spend the major part of my holiday there because my mother lived there and two brothers of mine too, until they were expelled in 1992 from Sanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, before the visit to Manjaca, when were you in Kljuc for the last time or in Sanica?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 I spent about ten days there, on several occasions, because I was on sick leave and getting ready to retire so I almost spent the year 1990 in Sanica and in 1991, I was there only a few times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1992, were you in Sanica or Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 5th of January, 1993, I was there for the first time, in Kljuc. That is when I took a convoy of provisions there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in certain areas of Bosnia, the Bosniaks organised themselves in armed units?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that you don't know that there was an organised resistance in the Kljuc region?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 22nd of June, 1992, you were at a meeting with General Talic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of February, 2000, on page 1, the last page, you said that Colonel Selak attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that occasion, Colonel Selak had already asked to retire, he had already submitted his request for retirement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, he had done so at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that Colonel Selak had already made a request for retirement at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him before the war, too, through my job. And on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with Colonel Selak in 1992 while he was still a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but only occasionally or by accident. When he was demobilised, then we would see each other more often.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that at the meeting of the 22nd of June, 1992, you were present or that -- at which you were present with General Talic, you received authorisation to deliver humanitarian aid to the detainees in the Manjaca camp? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The General Talic quite correctly said that in further contact with Colonel Vukelic and Colonel Gojko Vujnovic, I should proceed with this, but mainly I carried out further work through Colonel Vujnovic Gojko. But the executive permission was given to me by the security organ, that is Mr. Dasic. And on this permission, it said, "Permission for movement in the zone of combat activities." Anyone going to Manjaca, the driver and the escort, had to have such a permission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions yesterday during the hearing, and in your prior statements, you said that you personally or through other members of Merhamet delivered aid to the detainees in Manjaca 48 times.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One plus 48. The first time at the negotiations and 48 times through the deliveries. For the first 15 times or so, I was involved personally. Later, occasionally, the rest was done by my associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about these 48 times, which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 18th of June until the first half of December, we went there the beginning of December for the last time, before Manjaca was evacuated, that is when the detainees were moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore, during six months, you delivered aid to the detainees in Manjaca 48 plus one, that is 49 times in that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: That means that you delivered such aid roughly twice a week?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you and other members of Merhamet each time were given permission of access to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that you were able to notice psychological change among the prisoners following the aid that you delivered to them.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once we started coming regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So following your visits to Manjaca, the conditions improved?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these visits were possible solely with the approval of General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His associates. I no longer had direct contact with General Talic for my visits. But it was on the basis of the general position of General Talic as expressed on the 22nd of June, which was fully observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that at the Manjaca camp, you spoke to Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the stable for a moment, for a second, and we spoke after representatives of the detainees came out of the stables, seven per stable, in the open area in the presence of the officers who were participating in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that Omer Filipovic died the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The night between the 28th and the 29th. That is what was written in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 3 of your statement of January, 1996? It is the last sentence in the one-but-last paragraph. You said that Omer Filipovic was killed on the 30th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of July, I learned that he had been killed, but the correct date is the night between the 28th and the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the 28th or 29th of July or August? Because yesterday, you said the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I misspoke. It's July.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also said that on the same day that Filipovic was killed, you had a discussion with Colonel Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a coincidence. It just happened to be on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the same statement of 1996, on page 5, the last paragraph, you said that you spoke to Colonel Vukelic on the 1st of August, 1992, that is two days after the death of Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the minor date errors, but the conversation was on the 29th and the killing in the night between the 28th and the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also told us that on the day that Omer Filipovic died, you felt that the relationship between the police and the Manjaca staff was disturbed.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I felt that the atmosphere had changed significantly and that something of major importance had happened, and that is what prompted me to talk to Colonel Vukelic because it was not the same kind of attitude that the staff had when we delivered aid to Manjaca after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us today that yesterday you didn't say that the relationship between the police and the staff had changed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I said that something strange was happening and it seemed to me that something was wrong and that is why I asked to see Colonel Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, on page 34 of yesterday's transcript, you said, or at least that is how it was translated [Previous translation continues]... "between the police and the personnel in Manjaca had been disturbed."

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really didn't say that. I said what I just told you, that I felt that something was wrong in the atmosphere, that something had happened, as that is what prompted me to look up Colonel Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the first major release of prisoners took place on the 10th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally or someone else from Merhamet request that these persons be released?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion, 105 persons were released.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know why these persons were released?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because of the rules according to the convention, those under 18, those over 60 years of age and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether the International Red Cross visited the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but after us. We first started going there and they arrived I think it was in July, mid-July, or the second half of July, and then independently from us, without any agreement with us, they went to Manjaca. There was no coordination between us. We went on our own and they, of course, went according to their own assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you had contacts with the International Red Cross after July, 1992, surely?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said continuously, from the beginning until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in August, 1992, 92 persons were released from the Manjaca camp at the request of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In August, that is probably the 65 sick persons who were transferred to England. I assume that is what you're referring to. Among them was Muhamed Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you are aware that at least one release took place from the Manjaca camp in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Manjaca camp was closed in December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know under which conditions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Red Cross took care of the large group of detainees that remained in Manjaca but somewhat earlier, about 500 people had disappeared from the Manjaca camp. Afterwards, through the International Red Cross, seven days later, I learned that they were in the Batkovic camp in the north eastern part of Bosnia. Those people from Batkovici were finally exchanged in October, but not all of them. Some of them were released earlier but the last group was exchanged in October, 1993, at Turbe near Travnik, a total of 158 of them, and I was present at that exchange, prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that simultaneously with the liberation of prisoners from the Manjaca camp, Serb prisoners should have been released from Croatian and Muslim camps?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently. In most cases, there were exchanges in smaller or larger groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Serb prisoners were released from Muslim or Croat camps when the prisoners were released from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed so but I did not have any specific information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecutor showed you a video clip. It is 468, P468. The sound is a very poor quality but it is subtitled in Serbo-Croat. This video was taped in 1992 and the Prosecutor showed it to the Chamber to show them the Manjaca camp. I should like to show you a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. few clips from that same video, from the moment when the Prosecutor stopped it yesterday and I should like to you read out the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the video be shown, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, can you read to us what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Upon arrival, he declared that no matter how depressing the thing may appear,the camp appears to have been correctly run."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Medic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. That's what I anticipated. Is Prosecution going to make re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to use one document because Madam Fauveau referred to a release of detainees from Manjaca on 20th August and we have this document, and I would only like to show this document to Mr. Medic and ask him to read a few entries in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a document that already has an exhibit number? Has it been premarked?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. It is document which is part of your binders, Banja Luka collection, and it was premarked as Prosecution Exhibit P415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, just let us have a look at it because I was not informed beforehand that this document was going to be made use of in this morning's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You may pass on the exhibit or the document to the witness, and -- I think we better keep it for the moment. Yes, Madam Richterova. Mr. Usher, please give the document to the witness. And perhaps Madam Richterova you would kindly explain to the witness what document or ask him to explain the import or the nature of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau referred to a release of witnesses in August, and she stated that it was on request of International Red Cross. Would you be so kind and read on page number 1, the last paragraph, starting in B/C/S ... [no interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I? "A list of 92 individuals for whom there is no evidence of executing or participating in combat activities probably and are quite ill and their appearance is attracting attention from the media and representatives of humanitarian organisations."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it is just that their appearance is attracting attention from the media and humanitarian organisation. Can I ask you to move to page number 7?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And read the entry under number 5?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 7 the numbers are 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, she is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, so please can you read the entry under number 25?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sadikvic Fadil, son of and Abdulah, born 1934 in Krasulje, arrested on the 2nd of June, 1992, high blood pressure, sciatica and stomach illness."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And entry on -- entry under 26?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Oreskovic, Ivan, son of Ivan, born 1934 in Sanica."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the last --

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Arrested 31st of May, 1992, has a heart condition. I know this person personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The entries relating to 2nd of June and 31st of May are entries for when these people were arrested, and 1934 is date of birth. And the release of these persons were arranged for 20th of August. So it is two, three months, after they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I do not have any other questions to this witness, and I would like to ask you to formally admit it in evidence exhibits which were stated yesterday and today. It's P467, P468, P469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These are the three statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was the sketch, the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The sketch has already been admitted yesterday, I think. 467.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to make sure that they were formally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But -- and then there was another document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The criminal charges which was 468 and 469 in the two languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And 468 was the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 468 was the video, yes. So. Yes. Now this has to be admitted as well. And I would suggest to you that you ask for the formal admission of Exhibit 451 for the purpose of the evidence of --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, and I want to ask to be formally admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This has been admitted already, I think, no? Yes. This has been admitted already. And are we in a position to check on line now in real time whether the other three documents have already been formally admitted yesterday? They weren't? So they are being formally admitted now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, it's only in that the Livenote is 451, it is, in fact P415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 415, yes. Okay. I think you can have it back. Thank you. So you can put your mind at rest that all the documents you needed to have admitted have been admitted now. Mr. Medic, the Chamber has got some questions for you. Judge Taya, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, according to your statement dated 30th and 31st January, 1996, page 4, paragraph fifth of English version, you had an official meeting with General Talic on 22nd June, 1992. The explanation of this meeting is, at least for me, rather abstract, lacks concrete and exact description of the conversation which took place at that occasion. So I have several questions concerning this meeting and related matters. First, was this the first meeting for you with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First and last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: According to your same statement, four days before this meeting, that is to say on 18th June, 1992, you visited Manjaca camp, and you wrote your report about the findings from this visit. Then my questions are as follows: You had already finished writing this report before the official meeting with General Talic on 22nd June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, already on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Did you have any intention to deliver that report to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a report written for the executive committee of Merhamet so that they should know where I'd been, what I did, and what should be done next regarding aid. There were various suggestions as to how the detainees at Manjaca should be assisted. It was not intended for public use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said in the same statement, "I also gave the military officers my general impression from the visit to Manjaca camp, in which I officially notified General Talic and his men about the claims by the prisoners that beatings were regularly carried out in Manjaca." Concerning this sentence, I want to know more precisely, minutely, the contents of general impression from the visit to Manjaca camp. Please reproduce at your best recollection, what you said to General Talic and others at that time.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we had conducted talks, that I was satisfied with those talks. If what was agreed is implemented, and that the detainees had said that they were being mistreated there, and what I had seen in terms of the condition they lived in in the stables and their appearance. I really did convey this in very -- very briefly, because there was no sense in any lengthy descriptions of the conditions there, as I assumed that General Talic was aware of them. Also, at the end, when we came to the end of our talk, I asked General Talic why telephone connections with the environs of Banja Luka had been cut and I remember well the answer, which was that it was a strategic question and though I'm a civilian and I don't understand strategy, but only humanitarian issues up to a point, I couldn't really understand what this meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: At the last line of this fifth paragraph of page 5 of the same statement, you said "Tadic is very present in private contacts, always makes promises of help," et cetera. Then how about General Talic's attitude at the official meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely as it says there, that is what I still think, what I still believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: His attitude was different between private meeting and official meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression of a man that I was talking to at that point in time and attending a meeting with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What promises General Talic made? Please describe more precisely.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we could implement the agreements through his associates at Manjaca, which actually did take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said also in the same paragraph, "But the promises never materialised." When and how you knew that his promises were never materialised?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been a reference to other circumstances, but regarding the steps taken in Manjaca, regarding the delivery of humanitarian aid, those agreements were honoured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: My last question is: How about the situation of food shortage in the municipality of Banja Luka during 1992, apart from the shortage of alcohol? How about the situation of other foodstuffs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to medical alcohol, not alcohol as alcoholic drinks. Gradually, this shortage of essentials increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, I think that brings to an end your cooperation with this Trial Chamber as a witness. I must thank you for your cooperation, for having been with us and for having testified. You may now withdraw, and I think the Prosecution, the office of the Prosecution will have -- have already arranged for you, made the arrangements for your return to your country. Is there anything that you require, any further, from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may withdraw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am back. Your Honour, the next witness, Mr. Dzonlic, is I think waiting, but before I call him, I think we need to do some swapping of seats because there are only two, but can I mention two administrative matters while I do that? The first is this: Yesterday, Your Honour and Defence counsel were informed that we had a third witness coming this week. It is absolutely right that I hadn't -- we hadn't given to Your Honours the statement but I think it will be handed to Your Honours today. My learned friends were aware that he was next on the list. He's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But that I don't think I'd specifically -- in fact, I know I hadn't specifically said that he would be here this week. The reason he's being here is because I didn't want to run out of witnesses in case, Mr. Dzonlic finishes on Thursday, which it seems to me is possible, this witness will be available to be called on Friday. He deals with a very limited aspect of this case and so I would hope that if necessary, my learned friends will find themselves in a position to deal with that evidence. He largely affects Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think I would -- you would find me behind you foursquare if you take this approach to make sure that in other words we don't find ourselves in a predicament say on Thursday afternoon Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or Thursday having no more witnesses, something that actually we discussed amongst ourselves yesterday when we realised that, by 11.00, we had finished with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Medic. However, there is also this agreement or arrangement that we had come to in the early stages of this trial whereby on Thursday of the previous -- of each week, you inform the Prosecution -- so basically if it is your intention to take these kinds of advisable precautions, I would suggest to be on the safe side to mention or include the name of the witness rather than to leave it out. At worst, what could happen is that the Defence would -- and you would find yourself in a position where that -- the evidence of that witness has to be postponed to the following week, which is no major tragedy at all. So we could easily live with that. On the other hand, if the name of the witness is not mentioned or indication is not given to the Defence, the week before, when Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau stand up and say, "We were not told," et cetera, I have to show total understanding and probably also give in to their objections. Even though I must say that as we go along, I'm appreciating more and more their cooperation and their willingness to cooperate even further. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's no excuse, but of course we didn't sit Friday, and we were doing a lot of reorganising of witnesses on the Thursday and that is why things fell through the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. In any case, yes, Mr. Ackerman has got something to tell us in regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention -- I'm sorry, I'm afraid we have made -- I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet, but I want to mention the next witness. Madam Fauveau told the Court yesterday she was going to be two hours so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's not here. I'm told he's going to be here for the resumed sitting at 11.00. Your Honour, there is one other matter I can raise in the interim but Mr. Ackerman wants to say something about the next witness, I gather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- this third witness that the Prosecution has coming this week, I have begun my work on that witness. I think it's unlikely that we would get to the point of cross-examination in any event on Friday, and therefore, any objection that I made yesterday regarding his appearance this week I will now withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think we can move forward, and at best we will probably get through direct examination of that witness on Friday. I doubt we will get to cross but if we do, I'll be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Madam Fauveau? I haven't gone through the evidence or the previous statements of this witness because they have just been given to me now. So I don't quite know whether he involves more one accused rather than the other. It seems I seem to note more the name of Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he's almost exclusively Brdjanin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to raise with regard to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's very helpful and I'm grateful to both counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is grateful too. What I suggest we do is we break now. Incidentally later on this morning, you will have -- we are handing out the decision on the humanitarian -- okay? So that should solve the pending -- that particular pending issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one other matter to raise but Mr. Ackerman I see is back on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard further to this third witness, I just want to make it clear that I'm not agreeing to a permanent modification of the Rule. Ms. Korner actually should tell us on Thursday who is coming the next week and we -- this is fairly easy to deal with but it could be difficult and I think it we should enforce the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it in the first place because what happened has happened but I don't get the message that this is going to be a tactic that is going to be resorted to. Far from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I mean as Your Honour will appreciate, it's not always difficult to gauge times. One -- poor Mr. Dzonlic has been waiting ten days now I think. Your Honour, may I mention witness 7.177, the journalist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There have been some further developments in this matter. The summons was issued to him last Saturday. His newspaper or his exnewspaper has instructed counsel who wishes to appear, not on Monday, the 4th for which the summons was actually issued, but on the following Wednesday. Now, Your Honour, the point that's been made and that's why I'm raising it at this stage to put Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman in the picture because it doesn't affect General Talic's case, first of all. But second, to again raise this question of whether it is required for him, the journalist, to give evidence. The reason I raise it is because I spoke to counsel who has been instructed, and he made again the point that the interview was in fact conducted through the interpreting services of another journalist who spoke the Bosnian language. The journalist who actually wrote the article did not, and therefore his article is based on the translation that was given to him by his colleague. Now, of course, Your Honour that's not uncommon. All the interviews effectively with witnesses that are conducted by investigators or lawyers are conducted through interpreters so to that extent I suppose they could be said to be hearsay. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the point that was made again was that Mr. Ackerman requires him to attend for cross-examination. If it is to be cross-examination upon the content of the interview, the journalist is going to say, "Well, I recorded what was translated to me but I can say nothing further about it." And therefore, Your Honour, this is going to be a time-consuming process and perhaps an unnecessary one. Again we are really asking Mr. Ackerman to reconsider the request that the journalist attend for cross-examination. We are content purely to put the article in that was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, of course, they are content to put the article in that was written because that would deprive me of any confrontation of any witness at all. If this witness could not understand what Mr. Brdjanin was saying, then I don't know how he can be a witness in any event, to anything. But certainly anything he wrote down that he couldn't understand Mr. Brdjanin saying certainly could not be evidence before this Court. Ms. Korner has touched the very matter that is the essence of my challenge, and that is that the person who could actually understand what Mr. Brdjanin was saying was hostile to Mr. Brdjanin politically and it's my contention that what was written down was not what Mr. Brdjanin said. And so I can't imagine how this statement could be admitted without me being able to confront the person who actually had the conversation with Mr. Brdjanin, whether it be Mr. Randall or someone else. And if it's true that Mr. Randall has no idea what Mr. Brdjanin said other than what someone else told him, then certainly the article can't come in and I'm sympathetic with the Prosecutor's problem but I have a right to cross-examine the witness who spoke to Mr. Brdjanin and understood what he said. That may not be Mr. Randall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not an a easy situation at all, because basically, you are -- Ms. Korner you are making a statement which is very convenient for Mr. Ackerman to agree with, to start with. In other words, that although the paternity of the article itself goes to this witness, this particular witness, in reality, the person who conducted the interview was someone else, and anyway, what is purported to be an interview here, according to what you are stating, is what the other person told this witness, this reporter, that Mr. Brdjanin had stated. More or less this is how it is. May I ask if the other person, in other words, the person who put the questions to Mr. Brdjanin in a language which Mr. Randall did not understand or could not understand, is going to be produced as a witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, interestingly enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without mentioning his name now obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Interestingly enough, the person who -- the fellow journalist who actually did speak the language is at the Tribunal at present. He has been spoken to before by someone from the Prosecution and declined utterly to testify. We are making efforts to speak to him again today, to see whether the position will change. Your Honour has mentioned, and rightly, that it's the best evidence that one should call but one has a difficulty particularly with journalists and particularly I have to say with American journalists who take a very -- or their papers take a very strong line about any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this other witness an American?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's an American journalist -- about testifying. We are making attempts to speak to him today in the hopes that he can be persuaded for the reasons that are obvious, that he is the actual person who interpreted. But having said that, Your Honour, the Prosecution would still submit that the journalist who wrote the article -- I hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say about the interpreter's hostility to Mr. Brdjanin, so-called, the person who wrote the article presumably will have satisfied himself in whatever measures a journalist can, that what was being reported was accurate. Now, Your Honour, all the reports of interviews, as I say, with participants in the conflict, and indeed witnesses, are always conducted through interpreters. That is one of the problems. And so to that extent, one is reliant on and it's one of the problems that has come up in the statement, on the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the difference that in those other instances there is a measure of control, while here, unless this witness is brought forward to answer questions or to enlighten us on the allegations that are being made by -- particularly by Mr. Ackerman, he was a person who either -- who was hostile to Mr. Brdjanin himself. It's a serious allegation. And unfortunately we don't get anywhere further or any further from what the position seems to be at the present time, at the present moment, I think we are still very much in the air. Because basically what you have is an article and an author that will come here and say, "Yes, this is based on what my fellow journalist told me, Mr. Brdjanin had stated in B/C/S." No way of controlling whether he was being taken for a ride or whether he was being told the truth by his fellow journalist. And there is this allegation that this fellow journalist, contrary to Mr. Randall, had an axe to grind -- I mean he was not sympathetic at all in regard to the accused Brdjanin. I don't need to say much more. You realise immediately the position in which the Trial Chamber would find itself. It will not say, "No, we will not admit this statement," but it doesn't take anyone much to realise how much importance the Trial Chamber will give to the statement after that. If the situation remains as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour as I say we are -- we hope to speak to the journalist in question this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was no one else present, these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand it, it was just the journalist who wrote that article and his co-journalist, who at the time interestingly enough was working for an English newspaper. Your Honour, I think it may help, I don't know, having said that, my previous dealings with American press do not give me great cause for optimism, but if Your Honour were to express the view, which I could express to him, that his testimony is clearly important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This other journalist?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To this other journalist, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has he been declared as a possible witness to the Defence or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As he been, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Indicated as a possible witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, by to you the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no because we have not spoken to him yet, but at the moment we know he's declined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What power does the Trial Chamber have over him at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None except if Your Honour were to express the view perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course I can express the view. I mean the importance of the witness -- of the testimony of such a witness is self-explanatory, it's very obvious if it's on the basis of what he told this other journalist that this article was drawn up and eventually published, the importance of him coming over is obvious. But whether you will get him to come here, come forward and give evidence is another matter. And you understand that we cannot force him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, not unless I formally apply for a witness summons, even though he's made no statement, he's clearly got material evidence to give, but at the moment I'd prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure it's helpful for to you say that it's important that he come testify because if you said the opposite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I said it would be useful, his testimony may be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's whether it is essential or not is another matter but from -- if Mr. Randall comes forward and says, "This was drawn up on the basis of what Mr. so and so or Ms. so and so told me after interviewing Mr. Brdjanin in Serbo-Croat," then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a matter that might have been better resolved in conversations between Ms. Korner and I rather than bringing it to the attention of the Court at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously but you are also not in a position to force this person to come over and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If he's here maybe the solution is for Ms. Korner and I to talk to him together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe, if you can find that solution together, I will leave -- let you sort things amongst yourselves, talk about it, discuss amongst yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See whether it is at all possible. Not very optimistic but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think instead of the Prosecutor going off to try to talk to him, that what should happen is they should try to arrange a meeting between he and Ms. Korner and I and we could have a very frank discussion about whether he will -- what it is he would be prepared to say and whether he's prepared to testify or not and chances are we could solve the whole problem that way rather than engaging in this kind of a contentious argument in front of Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially if he gets word that you said he was not sympathetic at all or he was antagonistic towards -- in regards to your client, I can see him literally rushing into this courtroom to give evidence. Anyway, I'll leave it up to you to see if you can find a solution. I don't think the Trial Chamber is in a position to do anything in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only reason I raised it so that Your Honour became aware that there was -- if the summons is -- well, it has been enforced, there is an application by counsel representing the newspaper for which Mr. Randall worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I think Mr. Ackerman has heard that so we can take it up from there. We will break now for half an hour. You said Mr. Dzonlic is coming at 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I hope he'll be here before that so he can settle in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's say we can resume the sitting at 10 or 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think if Your Honour were to say 11.00, we would definitely have him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Dzonlic is in the waiting room. I think the usher has gone to get him. We need the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Mr. Dzonlic, you are now going to be given a statement that you are kindly asked to make before you start giving evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, as you may have gathered already, I am the Presiding Judge and I am flanked by the other two judges forming this Trial Chamber. To your right is the team of lawyers for the Prosecution that will be starting examining you this morning. To your left there are the two teams for the Defence. The front row there is the team for the Defence of Mr. Brdjanin and the back there is the Defence team for General Talic. Ms. Korner you may proceed

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you give your full name to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: My full name is Amir Dzonlic. My father's name is Kerim and my mother's name is Behija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, are you a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not that it needs saying, but in other words, of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I am of Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, before we deal with the matters that you are going to testify about, can I just deal with the documents that you have seen before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that you arrived in The Hague not last weekend but the weekend before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity on Sunday over a week ago to look at the B/C/S translations of the statements that you had made to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was allowed to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, was last Sunday the last time that you looked -- read through those statements?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition, did you look again at some of the documents you had looked at when you made your second statement?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is this the situation that the information that you provided in your statements is now given from memory of the events and meetings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the time, however, did you make notes of meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you attended a meeting, would you make a note as to what happened at the meeting? I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I did make notes sometime ago regarding all the meetings that I had in the course of 1992, and I made those notes in a diary in which I noted all the meetings that I had until the 26th of February, 1993, when I left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you still have a copy of that diary?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I don't have that diary because maybe in January, 1993 already, I destroyed it. I burned it because I was afraid to keep it among my documents because in it all the meetings were chronologically listed, meetings with certain people that I was in contact with, and I think had I succeeded in keeping that diary, it would have been much easier for everyone here present in the courtroom, but out of fear, I had to set fire to it and destroy it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzonlic. Now, Mr. Dzonlic, you told the Court that you left Banja Luka in February of 1993. For how long before that had you lived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I lived in Banja Luka since my birth, the 30th of October, 1959. That it means for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, please, to have a look at a map of a town plan of Banja Luka, which is Exhibit P2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wonder if it could be placed on the ELMO? Your Honour I think it may be better if he has a clean copy because that has quite a lot of annotations on it. Sorry. Your Honour, what we are now showing him is P2.1. It's a slightly different version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you indicate to the Court whereabouts you lived, by pointing on the plan you see next to you? Mr. Dzonlic, if you turn to the right --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: [Indicates] I lived in Banja Luka, in the district called Hiseta, in Djure Djakovica Street which can be seen here on the map, Hiseta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest straight away that he be given a pen, possibly in read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usher please give him, give witness a pen in red, red pen, and he will kindly circle the area where he used to live or the area he is indicating to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and could you kindly put your initials against that circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we remove the map from you, Mr. Dzonlic, was there a mosque near where you lived?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the immediate vicinity, there was a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: We called it Potpecinska Mosque. Its real name I think was the Sultan Mosque, but we called it the Potpecinska. That was the commonly used name for that mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you indicate to us on the map where that was situated?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Put a star this time, please, or a cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as that's another version of the map, could that be marked P2.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd ask that that be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, can you tell us what your profession was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Just now I'm adviser to the secretary of the government of the Federation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but otherwise, I am a former attorney. Prior to leaving Banja Luka I was an attorney at law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you qualify as an attorney?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: In 1989, I passed my bar examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From 1990 -- I'm sorry, from 1990, were you in private practice in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of work did you specialise in?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Most of my cases or 80 per cent of my cases had to do with property litigations and 20 per cent were criminal law cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As with most males in the former Yugoslavia or if not all, did you do military service in 1986?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in the former JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you join the SDA political party?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did join.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when did you join?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think it was -- I don't know the exact date but prior to the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you become a member of the SDA executive board in Banja Luka? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I became a member of the executive board of the SDA for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself stand for election to either the Municipal Assembly or the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I never was a candidate for state authorities either at the municipal or the republic level. I was only a member of the executive board of the SDA for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just, if we finish the list of your appointments, did you become, after your departure from Banja Luka, a member of the -- what was called the Banja Luka War Presidency, which was made up of Muslim and Croat persons?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the War Presidency of Banja Luka municipality, headquartered in Sanica, Travnik and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, I think, you were also for a short period of time a Judge of the District Military Court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked there from the 30th of March, 1993, until the 30th of September, 1993, as judge of the District Military Court of Travnik district.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, between October, 1993 and December, 1995, did you become the secretary of the Assembly of the Banja Luka district with its seat in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was secretary of the Assembly of the Banja Luka district, provisionally based in Travnik, right up until the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to the events of 1992. First of all, did you know Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't know him but I would see him and I could say that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I would see him on television and I would also see him in person in the municipal hall of Banja Luka municipality, in the cultural centre building, and I would most frequently see him in that building where the official premises of the SDS were situated. SDA also had its official offices in that same building for a time. That is the cultural centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what capacity did you first become aware of him? In other words, what position, as far as you were aware, did he hold?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I attended assembly meetings and Mr. Brdjanin at the time was a deputy in the Republican Assembly of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a deputy representing the SDS and I knew that he was a member of the republican parliament in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that he was a deputy representing the SDS. Do you know for which area?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: For the area of Banja Luka, for the Banja Luka region, on behalf of the region of Banja Luka. I think that he was on the SDS candidates list on behalf of Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where Celinac is?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Celinac is -- is it east Banja Luka? Towards Kotor Varos. It's a small town some 15 or 20 kilometres from Banja Luka along the Vrbana River.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Celinac came within the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Celinac is part of the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you attended assembly meetings at which Mr. Brdjanin was present. Were those assembly meetings -- I'm sorry, where were those assembly meetings? In Banja Luka or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Those meetings were held in the large hall in Banja Luka, in the cultural centre there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're talking, are you, about municipal assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know in what capacity Mr. Brdjanin attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly in which capacity, but as far as I know, republican deputies were duty-bound to attend municipal assembly meetings of the territory from which they came. In this particular case, as he came from the territory of Banja Luka municipality, it was his duty as a republican parliament member to observe and monitor the work of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of an organisation called the Association of Municipalities of the Bosnia Krajina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I heard of that organisation, the Community of Municipalities of Bosanska Krajina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, as it was called?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of the assembly was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any connection between Mr. Brdjanin and that assembly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Officially, no, but I heard, and there was talk that he too was in that Assembly of the Autonomous Region of the Community of Municipalities of Krajina, but officially I never learned that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you saw Mr. Brdjanin on the television or heard him on the radio. When did you first hear him on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. He didn't say that he ever heard him on the radio. His statements was that he saw him on television and in person. That's what the transcript will reveal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you ought to rephrase your question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
