utterances.text: Your Honour, I was looking for it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did mention TV, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's start -- well, I should ask you: Did you ever hear him on the radio?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of him on the radio?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Maybe towards the end of 1991, and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about on television?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I saw him on television earlier on too, because the parliament of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was constituted after the first elections in 1990. And I saw him, I can't give you a precise date, but given that whenever there was an assembly meeting, I would see him too because I would follow the sessions of the assembly and I would see him too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the kind of things that Mr. Brdjanin was saying, first of all, on the radio, at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell you that right now. I couldn't tell you precisely what he was saying towards the end of 1991. What I know he said, whether it was in 1991 or 1992, I'm not sure, but I know what he would say on the radio, but whether it was in 1991 or at the beginning of 1992, I can say what I heard he said on the radio, but whether it was in 1991 or in 1992, I don't know exactly right now, but I do know that he said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think the witness has said that he can only say what he heard that Mr. Brdjanin had said on the radio. I think that's getting a little bit far afield. He was asked what he himself heard and now he's apparently saying that he can't say that he himself heard anything but only what someone else told him that they had heard. And I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not my understanding either. Mr. Dzonlic, the question you have been asked and which you are requested to answer is, you have already stated that you heard Mr. Brdjanin make statements on the radio and on TV. Now you're being asked precisely, with reference to a particular time, what these statements were, and you are answering that you know what the statements were and you can tell us about them but not with a particular reference to end of 1991, or beginning of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. I didn't say that I had heard someone telling me this. I personally heard what Mr. Brdjanin said. I simply can't say whether it was in 1991 or in 1992. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps now you can answer the question that was put to you and tell us what you personally heard Mr. Brdjanin say on -- state on the radio any time it may have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the radio, Mr. Brdjanin, and not only on one occasion but on several occasions, said -- he called the Muslims balijas. "They don't have to prepare food for the winter, they don't have to prepare sauerkraut and prepare food for the winter because they are not going to remain here." We don't need wood for the winter for heating because we wouldn't be there. He said that in the territory of Banja Luka, sometimes he would say 3 per cent, sometimes he would say 5 per cent, of Muslims can remain in this territory. He would say that, "Wherever there is a Serb grave, that is Serb land," and he said that we were breathing Serbian air. I heard this personally on the radio. For a certain time, there were even comments in the daily news papers in Banja Luka in Glas, and they commented on his statements in which he would say that in the territory of Banja Luka, a maximum of 5 per cent of Muslims could remain. He called us Muslims and that is the derogative term for -- he called us balijas and that is a derogatory term for Muslims. He said that if his father, who is over 80 years old could work in the garden, then balijas could also work, they could also do work obligations and carry out hard work. I can't remember what else he said at the -- at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about on television? What were his speeches like or what was he saying on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if this could be put in a time context again, Your Honour, so that we know that it's within the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, the -- you've told us that you became aware of Mr. Brdjanin making speeches towards the end of 1991 for the first time. When dealing with appearances on television, what period of time was that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think that was the first time -- that the first time he appeared on television was in 1991 and these speeches which I have mentioned now, they were, I think, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Appreciating it's a long time ago, when you say 1991, what period of the year, roughly, did these speeches start?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the last quarter of the year, in -- from September until the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The speeches that you have described, the types of things, were those said on radio and on television or more on one than the other?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: More on the radio, on the radio. And as far as I can remember, on television, he spoke about the formation of the Assembly of the Serbian People, about the necessity to form an Assembly of the Serbian People, and the insulting remarks which he made with regard to Bosniaks were made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was anything said about those of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: He called the Croats Ustashas, he called them Ustashas. In fact, he would always call them Ustashas, because in historical terms, the Ustasha had inflicted a lot of harm on the Serbs and he would always emphasise this and call all the Croats Ustashas, probably in order to incite national consciousness among all the other Serbs so he also called them -- used a derogative term for the Croats. He called them Ustashas. He never even called them Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What effect did those speeches, things said by Mr. Brdjanin, have on you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: It was terrible. It was awful. I -- at the beginning I personally could not understand it, but this provoked great fear, not only in myself but in others too, in all people. At the beginning, the people were accepting this but they were uncertain about this, but then they all became very worried because this was a cause of great fear and uncertainty among all the citizens who were of non-Serb nationality in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Brdjanin, were you aware of any other political figures saying things like that? Like the matters you've quoted?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I know that Andjelko Grahovac said that -- and I'm quoting him, "We don't need workers. We need warriors." And on this basis, I think that he expelled 90 -- dismissed 90 per cent of people from their jobs. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't know whether the name of the company is Universal, I can't remember. He also said that the Croats were Ustashas. Every time he was on the radio he would say that the Croats were Ustashas, but I can remember his statement, "We don't need workers. We need warriors."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us who was Mr. Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grahovac was the director of the firm which I think is called Universal, but he is a neighbour of mine with whom I grew up until the age of 30. He lived three floors above me. And there is one piece of information about him which is very interesting. His brother, Rade, committed suicide because he couldn't bear what his brother was doing and the side his brother had moved to. He killed himself. He couldn't bear this. And a second thing is that that Andjelko Grahovac married a Muslim woman, who was married to my colleague and neighbour Almir Smajic. Andjelko Grahovac was their best man and one year later, Aida, his wife, divorced her former husband, Almir Smajic, and he married Aida.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I stop you? It's my fault entirely, Mr. Dzonlic. What I wanted to know is, did he have any -- did Mr. Grahovac have any political position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think that he was a member of the core leadership of the SDS in Banja Luka. The municipal board of the SDS in Banja Luka. And he was appointed with this function as director of Universal and the director of the football club Borac Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, please, in 1992, were firms state-owned or privately owned or a mixture of the two?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were state-owned, state-owned. It was still a socialist system and state-owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've told us about Mr. Grahovac, was there any other politician or somebody in political life whose speeches or words you remember?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I remember the words of the president of the SDS, in the municipal organisation of the SDS in Banja Luka, Vukic, I don't know his real name. I can't tell you his real name now. He was a doctor and he worked in the clinical centre in Banja Luka. I know that he said that "Balinkas and Turkish women will never give birth again in the hospital, in the clinical centre."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move -- I'm sorry, before I do that, anybody else that you can now remember who -- in particular, who was making speeches like this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember anyone else now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I want to move, please, to another topic. The topic of mobilisation. After the war with Croatia started, in June, 1991, was there a mobilisation call in September of that year?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who issued that mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: There was a public call-up through the media, through the radio in Banja Luka, and through announcements in the municipal, daily bulletin called Glas. There was a general call-up, a general mobilisation which had been issued. And it was considered that everyone was being called up for mobilisation on this basis and later there were individual call-ups for each conscript from the municipal secretariat for the Defence, the national defence of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the answer is not responsive at all. The question was, "Who issued the mobilisation call?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Mr. Dzonlic, you would direct your attention to answering the question, the whole question and nothing but the question, and in fact, Mr. Ackerman is partly right. You have not given us the proper answer to the question that was put to you by Ms. Korner. Could you answer that question now, please? Are you in a position to tell us who --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can put a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is also an issue of how is a mobilisation call in 1991 relevant to an April through December, 1992, indictment? Ms. Korner may have an argument that it is but I can't see it and I would object on that basis also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that objection, and as far as it is based on what you've just stated is dismissed. Ms. Korner can definitely -- either rephrase the question or even put a direct question, because this should not be controversial in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I'm asking is because it's going to lead into the next aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, can I just change the question? Who had the authority to issue a call for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The relevant Municipal Secretariat for National Defence proclaimed the mobilisation and sent the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In September of 1991, who actually issued the call for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Secretariats for National Defence did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did those of Muslim ethnicity respond to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Some of them did respond but most of them didn't. Most of them didn't respond to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Croats? Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The Croats also didn't respond to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those who failed to respond, were any proceedings, any proceedings, taken against them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who took those proceedings against them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The proceedings were instituted, it depended on the persons or the people who were in question. At the time, if a Croatian citizen did not respond to the mobilisation call, then against such a citizen, proceedings would be instituted before a military court; whereas, for Bosnia citizens, a misdemeanour case would be instituted in front of the municipal court for misdemeanours in Banja Luka at the proposal of the Secretariat for National Defence, who would submit to the relevant courts a request to institute proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about those of Serb ethnicity who did not respond?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not a single Serbian citizen was subjected to proceedings of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you play any part in the legal proceedings taken at that stage against those of either Croat or Bosniak ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I defended quite a few of these people, as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 199 -- were these proceedings taken in 1991 after September?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the result of those proceedings in cases in which you acted?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: In all the cases or in the majority of cases in fact, I raised several objections, depending on the case, but the final outcome of these cases was usually, as far as Bosniaks are concerned, who were tried at the misdemeanour court, they would be fined or they would be sent to prison. In the cases where I defended certain Croats before the military court, the proceedings were not brought to an end and I don't know what happened to them, not completely. I know that I appealed to the council in these proceedings against certain men. I appealed against a judgement for certain men. And I filed this appeal with the high courts. I don't know what happened to them in the end because I left Banja Luka so I don't know how these cases were finally concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, once the conflict broke out in Bosnia, were there further mobilisation calls issued?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who issued that call for -- or those calls for mobilisation and when was the first, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The call was issued by the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence but I can't remember the date when the first one was issued. Perhaps if I could look through my cases, I could find it out, but at the moment, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did Bosniaks respond to that mobilisation call in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Most of them did not respond. Some Bosniaks did, those who received the call-up at their place of work, they responded to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what happened to those who failed to respond?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Those who failed to respond to the call-up for mobilisation would very quickly lose the right to work and after that, they would lose their entitlement to an apartment, and they had no other choice but to leave Banja Luka. And there were also some who were beaten up because they failed to respond to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the -- was housing and employment connected in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: If someone lost his job, then his company would immediately deprive him of the right to an apartment, because the apartment was owned by the company that had given that apartment to the worker to use. So once he lost his job and was dismissed, he lost his employment, then the company in which he worked would deprive him of his right to an apartment so there was a link between employment and housing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, did you act for people who failed to respond to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did represent them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just Bosniaks or Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Both Croats and Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At which court did the Bosniaks and Croats appear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: It depended on the type of case. They would appear at the Municipal Magistrate's Court in Banja Luka, at the Military Court in Banja Luka. This court was called the Military Court of Zagreb based in Banja Luka. And at the higher court in Banja Luka, that is the Court of Associated Labour, which dealt with the legal employment issues. And sometimes I also wrote appeals to the supreme military court in Pale. So I would appeal certain cases at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that in 1991, the Croats had gone before the military court and the Bosniaks before the civil court. In the 1992 proceedings, was there a distinction between Croats and Muslims as there had been in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a distinction. But now things changed. It was the Bosniaks now who were sent to the military courts and the Croats to the civil courts, the magistrate courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the difference between the military court and the civil court, in terms of penalty?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The penalty in the civil courts was in the form of a fine or a prison sentence up to 60 days; whereas, in military courts, the penalty could be up to ten years for failure to respond to a mobilisation call-up. I think it's -- it was stipulated up to ten years. I'm not quite sure of that because it was a long time ago, but in any event, the penalties in the civil courts was a fine and a sentence up to 60 days; whereas, in the military courts, the envisaged penalty was up to ten years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people who you represented at the military court, what was the average type of sentence that they were receiving, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I don't know, as I have said already, what finally came of all those cases because I had to leave Banja Luka, but I do know what happened with some cases, because I did represent people at the military court and they were sentenced between 4 and 12 years of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In view, as a lawyer practising in Banja Luka in that in 1992, was the mobilisation order a legally issued order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object that he's not been qualified to -- as a legal expert to give an answer to that. That's a fairly sophisticated legal question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, why are you asking this question? What's the relevance to the rest of your examination-in-chief? Or what are you trying to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that in his statement there is a substantial part in which he more or less gives us his personal opinion as a lawyer on the legality or -- of several decision that is were actually taken. Some of which are very much constitutional matters, constitutional law matters. I don't know what's the utility of having a witness telling us whether a particular decision was considered to be legal or not. I can see some relevance, mind you, but I would like to hear you tell me what is precisely what you're after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the allegations in the indictment is a denial of fundamental human rights. The evidence that Mr. Dzonlic is giving about the sentences that were being meted out by this court as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. result of a failure to respond to a mobilisation, that we submit was in the circumstances, certainly from the legal -- the lawyer's point of view, an illegal one, is a matter that Your Honours should be considering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, why don't you rephrase the question and ask him whether at any time he, as a lawyer, contested the legality of -- and we leave it at that? Because, I mean, I don't fancy being told by the witness for sure whether this was a legal decision or not. I think we could live with having it rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, did you at any stage contest for your clients the legality of the order to respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was my grounds for appeal, for my objections and the appeal, because the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had passed a decision that only the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was competent to proclaim a mobilisation, and not the municipal secretariats. And that was my first and only grounds for challenging the Court decisions whereby my clients were found to be guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask him now whether he maintains that position today, after ten years, or whether he himself has doubts about the legal stand taken by him in defence of his clients at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, did you hear His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it. I fully abide by that position even now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But does -- you are a lawyer too, sometimes in defending our clients, we do not necessarily believe in what we state, by way of defence. So you stand by that position even now -- today, ten years after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to this day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, then, and just to complete that, you still have in your possession a number of files relating to clients of yours in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have them in my possession. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you have been unable to find these clients in order to obtain their permission to release them?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I was not able to find those clients, but I do know that when those clients came to see me in 1992, each of them said that they wanted me to pursue the matter right up to some international court, that is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we turn next, please, then, to the events in April and May of 1992? Do you recall an organisation calling itself the SOS arriving in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think it was for Bajram in 1992. I cannot tell you exactly which month or date that was but I know that it was Bajram in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was the first -- or how was it you first became aware of the presence of this organisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: One morning we woke up and on the radio it was stated that the SOS had taken over power in Banja Luka. That was the first time I heard of SOS. I'd never heard of it before, nor did I know what it meant. They said the Serbian defence forces are taking over power in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What physical effect did that have any -- did that have, if any, on, for example, movement in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Movement was unimpeded, there was no prohibition on movement. However, virtually at every major crossroads and at every more important building in Banja Luka, there were guards and barricades, bunkers made out of sand. So that even this in itself was sufficient to impair the freedom of movement of people, but officially it was not prohibited, as far as I can remember. Nobody said that we were not allowed to move around. But they gained control of all the more important facilities, ranging from roads to the economic facilities, the Privredna Banka, the post office and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the members of this so-called organisation, the SOS?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I did, in the street, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Most of them were wearing military uniforms, but there were some also wearing camouflage military uniforms, others camouflage police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the difference between military camouflage uniform and police camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The military camouflage uniforms are greyish olive, combined with brown. And the police are more bluish; they are camouflage, but the dominant colour is blue. That is what I inferred because the police always wore blue uniforms and the military olive-grey uniforms. That is how I knew which was which.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you saw the -- these members of the SOS, where did you actually see them? I mean, you said in the street, but anywhere in particular?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I saw them down the road in which I live. When you go to the main street, Titova Street, which is the main street in Banja Luka at the crossroads, there was a police car. It was parked in the middle of the intersection of. Then I went on to towards the Privredna Banka on the bulevar in the centre of town. I saw them next to the bank. A bunker was made out of sand and they were there too and also on the bank building itself. I saw them next to the post office. That is where I passed by and where I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I did. I said as soon as I left my street and got to the main street at the crossroads, there was the regular police, the police car with the word "Milicija" written on it. This was a regular police car.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did members of the regular police, that you ever saw, make any attempt to remove the barricades?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: There was no barricade there. They were standing in the middle of the intersection as some sort of a warning, indicating that something was going on further down the road. There was no barricade there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's my fault. You're quite right, Mr. Dzonlic. You said the word "bunker," that was further down the road, a bunker made out of sand near the bank.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Down the road, as you're going to the centre of the city, there was the Privredna Banka and there was this what I call a bunker, and next to the bunker were probably these SOS members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever see members of the regular JNA dealing with any of these SOS forces?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: At the time, I thought that they were members of the regular army, because I was not aware of the existence of this SOS because they were wearing the uniforms of the former JNA. So I saw them as being regular JNA members. That was my opinion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the Banja Luka Corps at that stage in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did know that the Banja Luka Corps existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were wearing this uniform, this camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During this period, were people able to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: At the time, no one could leave. I didn't see it but I know that there was -- it was said that Banja Luka was blocked, that is, all entry and exit points were blocked, and that no one could enter or leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, for how long did this SOS force, whatever it may have been, remain in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think not for long. Maybe a couple of days. Maybe a couple of days. And then allegedly the legal authorities took over control. It may have lasted five or six days. I cannot be specific but I know it didn't last long. For a few days only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now I want to move to a different topic. Have you heard the expression "Crisis Staff"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of the expression "Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was the first time in 1992 that you heard the expression "Crisis Staff," roughly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think it was in May, shall we say? May, month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you become aware of such a thing?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: There was stories -- there were stories in Banja Luka about the Crisis Staff, and also individuals who brought me decisions, that is on the termination of employment, and they brought a copy of that decision, and it said, "Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina," and that is how I officially saw that the Crisis Staff existed. That is, on the basis of the documents and the decisions my clients brought with them to my office, sometimes they had these decisions with the heading, "Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before your clients brought you a copy of these decisions, and I'll deal with that in a moment, had you heard anything about the existence of the Crisis Staff in the media?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think I did, but I'm not quite sure. I think I did. I think that the media also referred to the Crisis Staff. I cannot be quite explicit, but I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of who was in charge of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I learnt that the main person in the Crisis Staff was Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you learn that? In other words, from official announcements or through people telling you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: From people telling me, but I also saw these decisions of the Crisis Staff which he had signed as the President of the Crisis Staff, and his name Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before -- I'm sorry, I'll rephrase that. The Crisis Staff that was headed by Radoslav Brdjanin was the Crisis Staff for what? In other words, what area?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was responsible for all walks of life, not just one aspect but for life as a whole in the territory of Bosanska Krajina, for all segments of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just elaborate for a moment on that? When you say, "All segments of life," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Ranging from the economy, information, agriculture, the use of power, electricity, education, culture, so the Crisis Staff took over all control over all aspects of life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before 1992, had you ever heard the expression "Crisis Staff" before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I had heard of the expression "Crisis Staff," the legal expression. And for me, this meant the formation of certain Crisis Staffs during emergency situations, floods, fires, earthquakes, that is what the term "Crisis Staff" meant to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And -- well first of all, let's deal with, you say fire or earthquake. Had there been a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka at a period before 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I remember my father talking about it. There was in Banja Luka a tragic, large scale earthquake in 1969 and that is when a municipal Crisis Staff was formed, because this was an emergency and it was a very powerful and destructive earthquake and a municipal Crisis Staff was formed, and I know that, though I was a little boy at the time, but I know my father talking about the formation of a crisis staff in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, before what I anticipate will be the break, from which walks of life would the Crisis Staff be formed? In other words, where would the members of the Crisis Staff come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that's improper, where the members would come from. We are talking about -- this case is about the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Does he know where the members did come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that would be the next question because more or less what I can gather from the sequence of questions that Ms. Korner is putting to the witness, she is intending to draw a distinction between previous existing Crisis Staffs and this particular Crisis Staff which was created for the purpose related to this case, so more or less whether, in other words, for this particular crisis period, a novel model of Crisis Staff was created. Am I right, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm trying to get at is there was a previous Crisis Staff and the composition of the Crisis Staff is one that is regulated, as I understand the matter, and this witness is in a position to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is relevant, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's talking about a municipal Crisis Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Staff in 1969, that -- with when there was an earthquake that was formed under a completely different set of laws than what we are doing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see if he can answer the question. He's a lawyer, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he knows whether the composition of a regular Crisis Staff is regulated or not, he can tell us. Yes, Mr. Dzonlic, please, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the previous Crisis Staff during the earthquake and before, until the beginning of this war that we had, I said that Crisis Staffs are formed in certain emergency situations. For Banja Luka specifically, when a municipal Crisis Staff was formed at the time of the big tragedy of the earthquake, the Crisis Staff was headed by the town mayor, ex officio, as the town mayor, and I think the president of the executive council or the municipal government, and certain representatives of the various secretariats and also representatives of the civil defence, and that is how the Crisis Staff was formed. In view of the fact that this was a large-scale disaster, the Crisis Staff that was formed during the earthquake included representatives of republican bodies, from Sarajevo, because the damage was vast and the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina probably financed some of the aid. Then there were representatives of the authorities from Sarajevo present as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one final question, then. You've mentioned the mayor, the town mayor. Is that the same position as president of the municipal assembly or is that a separate position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: It is the same position. What I meant was the president of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will break now for half an hour. We will resume at 1.00 sharp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before the witness comes in, I know that this morning I was handed the response of the Prosecution to the motion by Defence teams for Biljana Plavsic and Krajisnik for the disclosure of documents in this case. I haven't come across any response from either you, Mr. Ackerman, or you, Madam Fauveau. Should I expect a response or can we go ahead? Go ahead, in other words, start --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You should not wait for a response, Your Honour. I think that issue is pretty well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- litigated in this Tribunal and I think the law is fairly clear as to how you should proceed. I don't see that it makes any difference to me. My view is they should have everything. There is an affirmative obligation for them to seek it out and I think they should have it. Under the same kind of protection that we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object to this request. As far as I'm concerned, as far as General Talic's Defence is concerned, all the documents and all the records can be forwarded to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can start working on that. The witness can be admitted now. You may sit down. Thank you. One further thing, Mr. Ackerman, and Madam Fauveau, this morning also I was handed a motion by the Prosecution for further protective measures. I suppose you are -- you have received that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've received it and I have no objections to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm putting the question to you because we can proceed very quickly on it. I don't think there is any controversy or there shouldn't be any controversy. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the decision will be handed in due course fairly quickly with the understanding that your request or your motion will be acceded to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm most grateful for that indication. In respect of the witnesses listed on the list for Sanski Most, which are Rule 92, we are going through the statements at the moment to see if there anything that we want to excise and we will then supply to the Chamber the English and the attested to B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So welcome back, Mr. Dzonlic. The Prosecutor will continue with her examination-in-chief. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, you've told us about the Crisis Staff that was headed by Mr. Brdjanin. Did you hear ever of another Crisis Staff situated in Banja Luka itself? I'm sorry, it's a bad question. Of another Crisis Staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard of the municipal Crisis Staff in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you aware who was the head of that municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I officially had no information on this but I assumed that the president of the municipal assembly, Predrag Radic was at the head of the municipal Crisis Staff. This was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that you had seen a copy of a Crisis Staff decision which was brought to you by one of your clients, more than one, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to look at a particular decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which Your Honours will find in volume 2 of the Banja Luka binders marked as P339. Now, Your Honour, I don't know how Your Honours's dividers run, but in my version it's the fourth number 17 and I'd ask that the witness -- I'm sorry, I've made a mistake. Just -- can I just check that for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it should be 339. Can I just have a look for a moment? I think that may be a -- no. It's definitely not that. Your Honour, I'm so sorry, can we try 202? I'm sorry, again, that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 202, I don't think that's the right one because 202 is the Security Service Centre --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, as usual my notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one, Ms. Korner, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry. It should be Exhibit 255. And I know what -- I wrote down the disclosure number by mistake, that's why. It's Exhibit 255 -- P255, disclosure number 3.39. That's why I wrote down P339 and it's actually -- that was the disclosure number. It's actually P254 -- 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we have a look at it, please? Because this was not one of the documents that we had prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right. I'm very sorry. Of course, you will have -- but it is actually still in volume 2, if you have volume 2 with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we just -- that's why we had picked the documents that were indicated to us so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll try to do better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we can -- yes, I think we can put it on the ELMO and that would make everybody's life easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could put the English version on the ELMO and we can hand Mr. Dzonlic the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, did you receive from one or more clients a copy of this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received such a decision from several clients, but perhaps I have the original decision. Maybe two or three original decisions of this kind. But I received them from several clients.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you were able, in fact, to provide a copy to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor who spoke to you, Kellie Ward?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this decision, as we can see, states that "Posts important for the functioning of the economy, may only be held by personnel of Serbian nationality." And goes on to state that "This refers to all socially-owned enterprises, joint stock companies, state institutions, public utilities and Ministries of the Interior and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These posts may not be held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed by plebiscite, or who in their minds have not made it ideologically clear that the Serbian Democratic Party is the sole representative of the Serbian people." Then it gives a deadline for the 26th of June, on which the presidents of the municipal Crisis Staff shall report it this Crisis Staff. "Failure to implement this decision shall result in the immediate dismissal of those responsible." And it's signed "Radoslav Brdjanin."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if we could turn it over on the ELMO, Mr. Usher, if that's all right, so that we could look at the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Will there be a question mark at some point? Is this a question or is Ms. Korner just reading the document to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There will be a question but the first question is to you, Mr. Ackerman. Is it accepted that this is the signature of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have given you a list of the documents and I can't tell you that just by looking at it. You have a list of the numbers that we agree are his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, how did -- what were the circumstances in which many of the clients were bringing you a copy of this decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: People would come to see me because they had been dismissed from their work after this decision, and they would bring decisions on terminating their employment in which reference was made to this decision. I told each client that if it was possible for the client, to provide me with this decision from its company, they should ask their employer to provide them with this decision. They would then go back to their company, and I don't know how they obtained this, they didn't all manage to obtain the decision, but quite a few of them brought these decisions to me on the basis of which their employment had been terminated, and the grounds for the termination were cited as this decision -- this decision was cited as the grounds for the termination of their employment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they bring, you, those who could bring this decision from their own firms, was it a photocopy?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the sort of people who were dismissed, first of all, what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What kind of firms or enterprises were they working for?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were working for social companies, socially owned companies, and they worked in public companies. There were colleagues of mine who were judges in the municipal court and who worked in Banja Luka. After this, they were dismissed from their posts as judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll deal with the judges in a second, but the clients, the non-judicial clients if I can put it that way, what sort of jobs did they hold?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were people who worked in schools, who were directors of schools or teachers in schools, and there were people who worked in companies. They had various jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were all your clients directors or in some kind of managerial position?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: There were some who held managerial positions. Mostly they held managerial positions, not directors but there were various chiefs in certain parts of companies, they formed part of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the judges that you have spoken of, what happened to judges who were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The judges who were Bosniaks were dismissed from their posts as judges because they didn't respond to the mobilisation, and in order to be appointed again by the assembly in Pale, they had to provide a certificate on having responded to the mobilisation. In other words, their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mobilisation was assigned to them at the court. This was their wartime assignment, but as far as I can remember, they also asked for certificates to show that they responded to the plebiscite of the Serbian people and this was a condition for them to be reappointed as judges at the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that the judges who were Bosniaks were dismissed. Was that all Bosniak judges?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Maybe in the first wave -- they weren't all dismissed, but at the end they were all dismissed. They weren't dismissed at the same time, all the judges weren't dismissed at once, but within about six months, they had all been dismissed. When I was in Banja Luka, I don't remember that there was a Judge who was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say they were all dismissed within about six months. What period of time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: That was from, let's say, May or June, 1992, until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about those of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: They were dismissed too. I can remember only one judge in the municipal court who was a Croat, and he's the only one who I remember worked as a Judge, and his name is -- I can't remember right now. He was there for the longest period of time as a Judge, and I know that he was later dismissed too and he is now living in Croatia, on an island in Croatia now because that's where he is from originally, and he's living on this island now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. We needn't trouble with his name. What action, if any, did you take when people came to you with these letters of dismissal?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: First of all, we wrote an objection to the employer in accordance with the legal provisions which were in force, according to which there was a deadline, I think it was eight days, within which we had to make an objection to the decision. Given that the employer often did not respond to this objection, to this complaint, and when he did, he would just confirm this first level decision on terminating employment, we would then file an appeal before the court of -- the so-called Court of Associated Labour, where they would deal with issues concerning employment, and its headquarters was at the high court in Banja Luka, as I said earlier on. On one floor there was the Court of Associated Labour and we appealed against the action taken by the employer and instituted legal proceedings. For a while, I waited, I waited for the court to respond to the appeals that had been filed, but the court did not respond. Let's say, for four or five months, they did not schedule any hearings. I wrote in writing to the president of the court, and said that a hearing should be scheduled, but they never scheduled a hearing for a certain issue, for any of the cases, and I think that they were hindering these cases from being heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In normal circumstances, in other words before this period, if there was an appeal against dismissal, how long would it take to be heard?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The customary time period was three months, and even that was long, but if you would address the president of the court or a president of the department in charge of a particular area with an official request as a representative of a particular client, then he would schedule it immediately. However, in these cases that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anyone for whom you acted receive a court hearing on an appeal before you left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to persuade any company to reinstate one of the dismissed Bosnian Croats or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: No, it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move now, please, to a different topic, and that is an association to deal with prisoners. Were you a member of an organisation called Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of Merhamet, but I was a member of an association which dealt with human rights, the implementation of the Geneva Conventions and prisoners within the territory of Bosnian Krajina, which was under the patronage of Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, did your organisation and Merhamet and other organisations have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First, can you remember roughly when that meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in April, 1992, in the premises of the Islamic Religious Community next to the destroyed Ferhadpasa Mosque in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, destroyed then or destroyed now?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: It was destroyed after that. It is destroyed now. Maybe a year after that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us which organisations were represented at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The representatives of the Islamic Religious Community were present at the meeting, representatives of the Cultural Muslim Society, Preporod, or rebirth, representatives of Merhamet as a humanitarian organisation of the Muslims, representatives of the Forum of Intellectuals of Bosniaks of Banja Luka and representatives of the Party of Democratic Action of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you recall who called the meeting, if not personally, which organisation was responsible for calling the meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who gave the initiative for the meeting and who was the organiser of the meeting but I can assume that it was the Islamic Religious Community and the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what makes you assume that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: That is what I think because it was held in the premises of the Religious Islamic Community, and I think that they were behind it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The purpose of that meeting was for us jointly to find ways of addressing all the problems we were facing at the time, and we were facing some terrible problems because people started coming to Banja Luka who had fled from the areas of Prijedor, Kozarac, Bosanska Gradiska, and they were recounting the horrors that were taking place in those areas. And after that, it was decided that we should rally all the Bosniak associations and try to respond in a certain way to all these things we knew were going on, and the aim of this meeting was to set up a commission for fighting for human rights for the implementation of the Geneva Conventions throughout the area of Bosanska Krajina which would be under the patronage of Merhamet. Those were the main aims of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? At the time of this meeting, you've told us that people had fled from Prijedor, Kozarac and the like, and were recounting the horrors. Was this meeting after the attack had taken place on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I think it was after the attack on Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Having made this decision to set up a commission, did you set up office premises?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: We decided where the office of the commission would be, and the office was in my former office where I used to work for a late attorney Sakan Rudin in Banja Luka, where I was an apprentice, in Fadil Maglic Street, number 4, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The commission, how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: The commission had four members, four members, representing these various associations, four members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us who the members were?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Members of the commission were Mr. Alija Hadzihalilovic from Banja Luka, an imam on behalf of the Islamic Religious Community; Mr. Bajric, Professor Bajric, I don't know his first name, representing Merhamet of Banja Luka; Mr. Adil Medic, as the representative of the Forum of Intellectuals; and myself on behalf of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we have to stop in about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have to stop in about three or four minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can finish this portion of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once your offices had been established, who came to see you at those offices?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who -- the offices were established, you told us, in the street. Did you receive people at your offices? Did people call at your offices?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. People would come on a daily basis. When they learnt about this office, they would come every day because in front of the office there was a large garden, and the yard was full of people, every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the help that they were seeking from your organisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Basically, they asked if we could find out information about their relatives, husbands, brothers, people detained, mostly at the Manjaca camp, and they informed us that there were camps also in Prijedor, such as Keraterm, Trnopolje and Omarska, and they asked us whether we could reach them, establish contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to Manjaca, I think, probably tomorrow morning but did you make any attempt to find out or to get information about the camps in the Prijedor area that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to inquire about Prijedor and Bosanski Novi and the Bosanska Gradiska and Bosanska Dubica. We did what we could to reach the competent authorities, people who were responsible for those camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any success in respect -- and we will take the municipalities separately, firstly Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC
utterances.text: We did not have any success regarding all these camps that I have listed and specifically Prijedor now, because we went to the Centre of the Security Services in Banja Luka to see the head of that service - I think his name was Zupljanin - with a request that he allow us to visit those camps. I personally went to the Security Services Centre with Mr. Adil Medic and Professor Bajric. We were turned back and we did not manage to reach Mr. Zupljanin. After that, Mr. Adil Medic and I think Professor Bajric managed to reach Mr. Zupljanin and I learnt, on the basis of what they told me, that Mr. Zupljanin had told them that they could not give them permission to enter Omarska, Trnopolje, Keraterm, stadium in Bosanski Novi and Bosanska Gradiska, but that we should go there to see the municipal Security Services Centres there, that is, the municipal police, and ask them for permission. However, as far as I know, for as long as I was in Banja Luka, they never managed to obtain permission, though we did keep on insisting, even through international organisations to be allowed to visit those camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Dzonlic, you are still in the position of a witness, so please, between now and tomorrow, do not get in contact with anybody with regard to these proceedings or the matters that you are giving evidence about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday the 27th day of February, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
